Design of a Microchannel Cold Plate for a 1 kW AI Accelerator

Nishant Subedi

Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of Virginia

Personal project · November 2026

Abstract

A direct-to-chip copper cold plate was designed for a 1,000 W accelerator die measuring 30 × 30 mm, cooled by 25% propylene glycol at a 35 °C inlet. A one-dimensional thermal resistance model built on laminar developing-flow correlations was used to evaluate 600 manufacturable channel geometries, and the design with the lowest pumping power that kept at least 12 K of junction margin was selected. The selected plate, with 150 µm channels, 100 µm fins and a 2 mm channel height at 1.0 L/min, gives a junction-to-coolant resistance of 34.2 mK/W, a mean junction temperature of 69.2 °C and a pressure drop of 12.6 kPa, for 0.21 W of pumping power. This is about 70% lower resistance than a conventional 1 mm-channel plate. Against the measurements of Tuckerman and Pease [1], the model predicts pressure drop and thermal resistance within 5% for their lowest-flux heat sink but deviates by up to 52% at higher flux, mainly because fluid properties are held constant. A finite-volume conjugate solution of the selected design agrees with the model within 4.6% in total resistance.

Keywords: microchannel heat sink; direct-to-chip liquid cooling; thermal resistance; laminar developing flow; electronics cooling

1. Introduction

Current AI accelerators dissipate on the order of a kilowatt from a die a few centimetres across. At that heat flux, air-cooled heat sinks cannot keep the junction within its limit, and most new server designs use direct-to-chip liquid cooling instead: a copper plate with fine internal channels is clamped onto the package, and coolant is pumped through it.

Narrower channels raise the heat transfer coefficient and the wetted area, but they also raise the pressure drop. The design question is therefore not simply how cold the chip can be made, but how much pumping power each degree of margin costs. This study builds a fast model for that trade-off, uses it to pick a design, and then checks the model against published measurements and against a more detailed numerical solution.

2. Problem definition

The target resembles a current GPU or ASIC: 1,000 W from a 30 × 30 mm silicon die, which is 111 W/cm² on average and about 220 W/cm² at hotspots. The coolant is a 25% propylene glycol–water mixture entering at 35 °C, and the junction must stay below 85 °C. The heat path runs from the die through a thermal interface material (TIM) into a 2 mm copper base, then into the fins and the coolant (Fig. 1).

3. Model

3.1 Thermal resistance network

The junction temperature is written as the inlet temperature plus the power times a series of resistances:

Tj = Tin + P (Rdie + RTIM + Rspread + Rconv + Rcal)(1)

Here Rdie and RTIM are one-dimensional conduction terms over the die area, and Rspread covers conduction and lateral spreading in the base, using a closed-form spreading resistance capped at the physical limit of no lateral spreading. The convective and caloric terms are

Rconv = 1 / [ h ( Abase + ηf Afin ) ],    ηf = tanh(mH) / (mH)(2)
Rcal = 1 / ( 2 ṁ cp )(3)

where Rcal accounts for the rise of the mean coolant temperature along the channel.

3.2 Convection and friction

The heat transfer coefficient comes from the fully developed Nusselt number for a rectangular duct of the given aspect ratio [2], with Stephan's correction for simultaneously developing flow [3]. Pressure drop uses the apparent Fanning friction factor for developing flow [2],

Δp = 4 fapp (L / Dh) · ½ ρ u²,    Wpump = Q Δp(4)

plus inlet and outlet losses. Fluid properties are evaluated once, at the bulk temperature.

3.3 Design sweep and selection

Channel width, fin width, channel height and flow rate were varied over 720 combinations. Designs were kept only if the flow was laminar and the fin aspect ratio could be made by skiving, which left 600. From these, the design with the lowest pumping power was chosen subject to a junction margin of at least 12 K (reserved for hotspots) and a pressure drop below 50 kPa. A two-dimensional finite-difference solution of the base, with a non-uniform power map and coolant warming along the flow, was then used to find the hotspot temperatures.

4. Results

Figure 2 shows the junction temperature and pumping power of all 600 designs. The selected design sits near the knee of the Pareto front; the coldest design in the set is only 7 K cooler but needs about 90 times the pumping power. Table 1 compares it with a conventional plate.

Table 1. Conventional and selected cold plate designs.

ConventionalSelected
Channel / fin / height (µm)1000 / 1000 / 3000150 / 100 / 2000
Flow rate (L/min)2.01.0
Junction-to-coolant resistance (mK/W)11534.2
Junction temperature, uniform power (°C)15069.2
Hottest hotspot (°C)—78
Pressure drop (kPa)0.712.6
Pumping power (W)0.020.21

In the selected design, convection is only about 7% of the total resistance (Fig. 3). Most of what remains sits in the die, the TIM and the base, so further narrowing of the channels gives little return. With three hotspots at roughly twice the average flux, the coolant warms by about 15 K along the plate and the downstream hotspot reaches 78 °C (Fig. 4). The sensitivity study (Fig. 5) shows that the benefit of higher flow fades beyond about 2 L/min and that each additional 1 mm²K/W of TIM resistance costs roughly 1 K.

5. Validation

5.1 Comparison with Tuckerman and Pease (1981)

Tuckerman and Pease [1] cooled up to 790 W/cm² from a 1 cm² silicon chip with water in channels about 50 µm wide, and reported measured pressure drop and thermal resistance for three heat sinks. The model was run at their geometry and conditions, with silicon and water in place of copper and glycol, and nothing was adjusted to fit their data (Table 2, Fig. 6).

Table 2. Model predictions against the measurements of [1]. Dimensions are channel / wall / depth in µm.

DesignFlux (W/cm²)Δp meas.Δp pred.R meas.R pred.
1 · 56 / 44 / 320181103 kPa103 kPa (−0.5%)110 mK/W105 mK/W (−4%)
2 · 55 / 45 / 287217117 kPa178 kPa (+52%)113 mK/W92 mK/W (−19%)
3 · 50 / 50 / 302790214 kPa261 kPa (+22%)90 mK/W76 mK/W (−15%)

Design 1 agrees closely. For design 3 the main cause of the discrepancy is the constant-property assumption: at 790 W/cm² the wall is near 94 °C while the bulk is near 34 °C, so the water near the wall has less than half the bulk viscosity. Evaluating viscosity at the peak wall temperature instead gives 159 kPa, which brackets the measured 214 kPa together with the bulk-property value. The thermal resistance comparison carries an additional uncertainty because the silicon thickness between heater and channel roots is not reported in [1]; it is worth about 7 mK/W per 100 µm, roughly 8% of the measured value. Design 2 could not be reconciled: it carries 38% more flow than design 1 through a smaller section, so laminar theory requires about 1.7 times the pressure drop, whereas the reported value is 1.13 times. The as-built channel dimensions would be needed to resolve this point.

The comparison suggests the model is reliable up to roughly 200 W/cm². The design in this study runs at 111 W/cm² with about 2.5 K between wall and coolant, well inside that range.

5.2 Finite-volume check of the selected design

The selected design was also solved with a finite-volume conjugate model of one half-channel (copper fin and base plus coolant, 8.8 million cells), combined with a three-dimensional conduction solution for spreading in the base. Results are compared in Table 3 and Fig. 7.

Table 3. Correlation model against the finite-volume solution for the selected design.

QuantityModelFinite volumeDifference
f·Re21.8121.770.2%
Channel pressure drop (kPa)12.5312.480.4%
Coolant temperature rise (K)15.215.10.4%
Convection resistance (mK/W)2.232.50−11%
Base spreading + convection (mK/W)14.613.1+11%
Junction-to-coolant total (mK/W)34.232.7+4.6%
Mean junction temperature (°C)69.267.71.5 K

The hydraulic quantities agree within 1%. The two thermal terms each differ by about 11% but with opposite signs, so the total agrees within 5% and the model errs on the conservative side. A 39-fold mesh refinement changed the convection resistance by 0.9% and the pressure drop by 1.0%. The finite-volume model assumes fully developed velocity (the entry length is about 0.6 mm of a 60 mm channel), neglects axial conduction and omits the manifolds.

6. Discussion

Three points stand out. First, once the channels are narrower than about 200 µm, the cold plate itself stops being the main resistance; what remains is in the die, the TIM and the base, which makes it a packaging and interface problem. Second, the coldest design is not the best one: the last 7 K costs about 90 times the pumping power, and that cost repeats for every accelerator in a rack. Third, because the coolant warms by about 15 K, the flow direction should follow the chip floorplan, since a hotspot placed downstream runs hotter than the same hotspot upstream.

The main limitations are constant fluid properties, a closed-form spreading resistance that is the largest single source of error in the model, and the absence of manifold maldistribution.

7. Conclusions and future work

A correlation-based model was used to select a microchannel cold plate that keeps a 1 kW, 30 mm die at 69 °C with 0.21 W of pumping power. The model agrees with a finite-volume solution within 5% and with published experiments up to about 200 W/cm². Planned next steps are a third independent result from ANSYS Fluent with the manifolds included, a manufacturable SolidWorks model of the plate, temperature-dependent fluid properties, replacing the spreading formula with the three-dimensional solution, and an assessment of thermo-mechanical stress in the TIM under power cycling.
